role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: Your Body Is Part of the Control System
summary: Your judgment runs on hardware: a body clock, a sleep debt and a stress response. This lesson teaches the two forces that set your alertness, why you are the worst judge of your own fatigue, and the rule-based controls that keep expensive decisions out of your worst hours.
body:
Mr Shabazz, your judgment runs on hardware. Two forces, the body clock and the pressure to sleep, decide how sharp you are at any hour, and because tiredness hides itself from the person who has it, the only reliable control is a rule set in advance, not a feeling checked in the moment.

Recall

Q. What is anchoring, and how do you defend against it in a price negotiation?

A. Anchoring is the pull the first number exerts on every estimate after it. You defend by writing down your own number, built from evidence, before you hear theirs.

Q. What does the outside view ask before you trust your own estimate?

A. It asks how a reference class of similar projects actually turned out, and starts from that base rate before adjusting for what is genuinely different about yours.

Q. What is a go/no-go gate?

A. A planned decision point where you either commit the next block of money and time, or stop, against criteria written down before you arrived at the gate.

Why this matters

A developer is the single point of decision on his own projects. The lender, the contractor, the architect and the lawyer all advise; you sign. A tired signature on a change order, a rushed reply to a landowner, or a misread line in a loan commitment can cost more than a year of careful work earns. You also work rotating shifts. That means some of your decisions will be made at hours when the human brain is built to be asleep. You cannot change the biology, but you can design around it, the same way a grid is designed around equipment that will fail sooner or later.

Two dials: the clock and the pressure

In plain English, two forces set how alert you feel. The first is your body clock, a roughly 24-hour internal rhythm that pushes you toward wakefulness in the day and toward sleep at night, with its deepest low in the small hours of the morning. The second is sleep pressure, a drive that builds every hour you stay awake and is discharged only by sleep.

The professional framing is the two-process model of sleep regulation, proposed by the sleep researcher Alexander Borbély in the early 1980s and still the standard way the field explains alertness. Your alertness at any moment is roughly the clock's push minus the pressure's pull. When the clock is low and the pressure is high at the same time, you are at your weakest.

Worked example one. Suppose, as a hypothetical, you wake at 14:00 for a night shift that runs 19:00 to 07:00. At 04:00 you have been awake 14 hours, so pressure is high, and you are sitting in the clock's deepest trough. That is the worst-designed hour of your day. If a contractor emails a revised price at 04:00 asking for approval by morning, the biology says the answer should wait. At 07:00 you have been awake 17 hours. A study published in the journal Nature in 1997 by Drew Dawson and Kathryn Reid found that after roughly that long awake, performance on a coordination task had fallen to a level comparable with drinking alcohol. You would not drive home after drinks. Do not sign a commitment after a night shift either.

You are the worst judge of your own fatigue

Plain English: tired people feel less tired than they are. The feeling of sleepiness levels off after a few days of short sleep, but the performance damage keeps growing.

The professional framing comes from a 2003 laboratory study led by Hans Van Dongen and David Dinges. People held to about six hours in bed a night for two weeks showed steadily worsening attention, eventually reaching deficits comparable to those seen after a night or more with no sleep at all, while their own ratings of sleepiness rose only modestly. The lesson for a decision-maker is blunt: your self-report is not an instrument you can trust. The American Academy of Sleep Medicine and the Sleep Research Society recommend seven hours or more for adults as a regular matter. Verify the current guidance against the primary source, and check your own needs with your doctor.

Worked example two. Suppose you sleep five and a half hours a night across five working days, against a need of seven. That is 1.5 hours short each day, so 1.5 times 5 equals 7.5 hours of deficit by Friday. One long Saturday sleep does not erase that in one night, and the research suggests recovery takes more than a single night. By Friday you will feel only slightly tired. You will be meaningfully worse.

Say that out loud now.

Say it this way: I am the worst judge of my own fatigue, so I decide by rule, not by feel.

Stress is a tool you can point

The third piece of hardware is the stress response: the faster heart, the sharper focus and the shallow breath before a hard meeting. It is not the enemy. Later this week you will learn two research-backed tools for steering it. The first is slow breathing, done only when you are parked or seated, never while driving. The second is reappraisal, which means relabelling the racing heart as fuel rather than as a warning. Your voice is the outward sign of all three dials, which is why the week ends on it. A tired, stressed speaker talks faster, higher and flatter, and the room hears it before it hears the words.

How the best do it

Industries where a tired mistake kills people have stopped trusting individuals to judge their own fatigue. Aviation authorities and many large operators run fatigue risk management systems: rosters designed around the body clock, limits on consecutive night duties, rest built into long operations, and a culture where a crew member can declare themselves unfit without blame. Many large contractors now apply the same thinking to long pours and night work, with hour limits and supervisor checks written into the site plan.

A one-person developer can copy the core of it for free. Write your own roster rules. Put your hardest thinking in your best hours. Make fatigue a reason you are allowed to give for asking for time, just as a grid operator can call for relief.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is an irreversible commitment made in the trough: a signature, a wire transfer, a price accepted on the phone, or an email that a court or counterparty could treat as agreement. The control is a written red window. For example: no signatures, no money moved and no new commitments between midnight and 08:00, or within eight hours of the end of a night shift, whichever is later. Anything urgent in that window gets one reply: I have this, and you will have my answer by 14:00. If the deal cannot survive that wait, it was not a deal you wanted to make tired.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner believes coffee and willpower close the gap. Caffeine masks sleep pressure for a few hours; it does not repay the debt, and it does not restore the judgment the debt has taken. The second beginner’s mistake is treating "I feel fine" as evidence. You now know that feeling fine is precisely what impairment feels like from the inside. If you suspect a sleep disorder, such as loud snoring, gasping at night or falling asleep at the wheel, that is a medical matter. Professional sign-off required: physician, ideally one trained in sleep medicine.

Callback

In Week 2 you built a decision journal: before a significant decision, you write what you expect, why, and how confident you are. Add one line to every entry from now on: hours slept in the last 24 hours and hours awake. Within a few months your own journal will show you whether your worst calls cluster after short sleep. That is the outside view applied to your own body, a reference class drawn from your own history rather than your hopes.

Recap

Two forces set your alertness: the body clock and sleep pressure. They combine worst in the small hours and after long wakefulness. Short sleep damages performance while hiding its own effects, so self-report fails you. The answer is a written red window, decisions routed to your best hours, and a fatigue line in your decision journal. Stress, breathing and voice complete the picture later this week.

Next: Ford, Failure Forensics, on the Exxon Valdez and what fatigue on the bridge cost.
checklist: Write your red window: hours and post-shift periods when you will not sign, pay or commit.
Prepare a one-line holding reply for urgent requests that arrive in the red window.
Add hours slept and hours awake to every decision journal entry.
Block your two sharpest hours each day for the hardest analysis and negotiation.
Track your actual sleep for two weeks against a seven-hour baseline.
List the symptoms that would send you to a doctor, and book the visit if any apply.
Tell one adviser or partner your red window so they can hold you to it.
head: Field checklist
speak: Two forces set how sharp I am at any hour. The first is my body clock, which pushes me toward wakefulness in the day and drops to its lowest point in the small hours. The second is sleep pressure, which builds every hour I stay awake. When the clock is low and the pressure is high, my judgment is at its worst. Research shows that after a long night awake, performance can fall to levels comparable with alcohol, and that people who sleep short feel only slightly tired while their performance keeps falling. So I do not trust my own sense of how alert I am. I decide by rule. I keep a red window: no signatures, no money moved and no new commitments in the small hours or straight after a night shift. Urgent requests get a holding reply and an answer by a stated time. I put hard thinking in my best hours, and I log my sleep in my decision journal.
terms: Circadian rhythm — the body’s roughly 24-hour internal clock that drives alertness up in the day and down at night.
Sleep pressure — the drive to sleep that builds with every hour awake and is discharged only by sleep.
Red window — a written personal rule naming the hours in which you will not sign, pay or make new commitments.

hostile.q: You work rotating night shifts. Why should I trust a developer who may be making calls on no sleep?
hostile.a: Because I do not leave it to feel. I run a written red window: no signatures, no payments and no new commitments overnight or within eight hours of a night shift. Urgent items get a holding reply and an answer by a stated hour, and my advisers know the rule. My decision journal records sleep against every major call, so I can show you the process, not just promise it.

title: The Exxon Valdez: Fatigue on the Bridge
summary: In March 1989 the tanker Exxon Valdez ran onto Bligh Reef in Alaska, and the US safety board named fatigue and excessive workload among the probable causes. This lesson takes the grounding through seven forensic steps and turns it into a rule about who is fit to make a critical call.
body:
The Exxon Valdez did not run aground because nobody knew where the reef was. It ran aground because the system around one tired officer assumed he would perform like a rested one, and nobody had a rule that said otherwise.

Recall

Q. In the two-process model, which two forces set your alertness?

A. The body clock, a roughly 24-hour rhythm with its lowest point in the small hours, and sleep pressure, which builds with every hour awake and is discharged only by sleep.

Q. What is loss aversion, and how does it distort a deal?

A. It is the tendency to feel a loss more sharply than an equal gain. It keeps people in failing deals to avoid booking a loss, and makes them overpay to avoid losing a site.

Q. What does a pre-mortem ask?

A. It asks the team to imagine the project has already failed and to write down why, before the decision is made, so that hidden risks surface while they can still be acted on.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, every development project has a bridge watch: the one person making a time-critical call while everyone else assumes it is handled. Often that person is you. The Exxon Valdez is the clearest public case of a disaster in which fatigue was formally named as a cause, and the mechanics of it translate directly to closing week, a concrete pour that runs overnight, or a lender deadline that lands the morning after a night shift.

Step 1: Timeline

On the evening of 23 March 1989 the loaded tanker Exxon Valdez left the oil terminal at Valdez, Alaska, heading out through Prince William Sound. After the harbour pilot left the ship, the vessel moved out of the normal outbound traffic lane to avoid ice reported in the area. The master then left the bridge, leaving the third mate in charge of navigation with instructions about when to turn back. The turn back was not made in time. Shortly after midnight on 24 March the ship struck Bligh Reef, and the resulting spill became one of the most damaging environmental disasters in North American history.

The US National Transportation Safety Board investigated and published its findings in 1990. Among the probable causes it named were the third mate’s failure to properly manoeuvre the vessel because of fatigue and excessive workload, the master’s failure to provide a proper navigation watch, and the shipping company’s failure to provide a fit master and a rested and sufficient crew. It also faulted the vessel traffic system and the lack of effective pilot and escort services. Read the report itself before you quote it, but that is the shape of its conclusions.

Step 2: Key decisions

Four decisions mattered. The decision to leave the traffic lane to avoid ice, which was reasonable in itself but increased the precision the next turn required. The master’s decision to leave the bridge during that manoeuvre. The third mate’s timing of the turn. And, years earlier and far from the ship, company decisions about how many people crewed a tanker and how much rest they got between loading and sailing. The last decision is the one most people forget, and it is the one with the longest reach.

Step 3: Assumptions

The system assumed that one officer could navigate a demanding manoeuvre, monitor position and manage the bridge, all at around midnight after a long working day in port. It assumed that rest happened somewhere in the schedule because the schedule did not explicitly forbid it. It assumed the traffic system ashore would catch a ship straying toward the reef. Each assumption was plausible on its own. Stacked together, they removed every margin.

Step 4: Incentives

Smaller crews cost less. Fast turnarounds in port earn more. A junior officer has little incentive to tell a master that he is too tired to take the watch. Nobody in that chain was paid to protect rest, and when nobody is paid to protect something, it erodes. This is not a story about bad people. It is a story about incentives that all pointed the same way, toward doing a little more with a little less, until the margin was gone.

Step 5: Warning signs ignored

The warning signs were structural rather than dramatic. Officers worked long hours in port during loading and then stood watches on departure. The board’s concern with crewing and rest shows that the industry knew fatigue was a hazard. The ice diversion was a known increase in workload at exactly the hour of lowest alertness. None of these was a secret. They were simply normal, and normal is the most dangerous word in safety.

Say that out loud now.

Say it this way: normal is not the same as safe, and tired is not the same as fit.

Step 6: Point of no return

The point of no return was measured in minutes. Once the turn back toward the lane was not started when it needed to be, a loaded tanker’s momentum made the reef unavoidable. Forensically, that matters: the decisions that could have saved the ship were made, or not made, hours and years earlier. By the time the danger was visible, it was physics, not judgment.

Worked example from development, and this is a composite example. A developer finishes a run of night shifts on a Thursday morning. His construction loan has a Friday funding deadline, and the contractor sends a revised schedule of values at 06:00 asking for sign-off so the draw can be submitted. He signs at 06:20. The revised schedule moves money from the roofing line into the general conditions line, front-loading the contractor’s payments. Three months later the contractor is struggling and the remaining budget does not cover the roof. The point of no return was 06:20, and it felt like routine paperwork.

Step 7: Root cause

The root cause was not one tired officer. It was a system that treated rest as something individuals would sort out for themselves, while every incentive squeezed it out. The individual failure was real, and the board did not excuse it. But a system that depends on a fatigued person performing perfectly at midnight has already decided to fail one night out of many.

Worked example two, the arithmetic of reliance. Suppose, as a hypothetical, a critical sign-off is done correctly 99 times in 100 by a rested person and 95 times in 100 by an exhausted one. Over a project with 40 such sign-offs, a rested decision-maker expects 0.4 errors and an exhausted one expects 2. The individual sign-off looks almost as safe either way. The project does not.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk for you is becoming the third mate on your own project: the one person holding the critical watch at the wrong hour, with no relief and no rule. The control is a fitness check before any critical task, the same way a lockout procedure precedes work on energised equipment. Before you sign, pay or commit, ask three questions. How long have I been awake? Is this the right hour? Who else could take this? If the answers are bad, the decision waits or changes hands.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner reads the Exxon Valdez as a story about one person who should have done better, and concludes that he personally would have. That is hindsight wearing a uniform. The useful reading is that well-trained people fail predictably under fatigue and workload, so the protection has to sit in the schedule, the crewing and the rules, not in anyone’s good intentions.

Callback

In Week 2 you learned the pre-mortem: imagine the project has failed and write down why. Run one on your own schedule. Imagine you made a costly error during a closing week. Ask what hour it happened at and how long you had been awake. Most people find the answer immediately, and that tells you exactly where your red window belongs.

Recap

The Exxon Valdez grounding moved from a reasonable diversion to an unavoidable collision in minutes, but the causes were laid down earlier: crewing, rest and a system that assumed fatigue would not matter. The fix is structural. Check fitness before critical tasks, design relief into the schedule, and let a tired person say so without penalty.

Rule 4: Before a critical decision I check fitness the way I check the numbers, and if the person deciding is not fit, the decision waits or changes hands.

Next: Roman, The Money, on what a tired mistake actually costs in carrying cost and return.
checklist: Name the critical watches on your project: closings, pours, lifts, funding deadlines.
For each, name a backup person who can take the decision if you are not fit.
Run the three-question fitness check before every signature or payment.
Never let a deadline you did not set override your red window without a reason written down.
Ask your contractor how long their crew will have worked before any critical overnight operation.
After any near miss, record the hour and your hours awake in the decision journal.
Read primary sources, such as the safety board report, before quoting a failure case.
head: Field checklist
speak: The Exxon Valdez ran onto Bligh Reef just after midnight on 24 March 1989. The ship had left the traffic lane to avoid ice, the master left the bridge, and the third mate did not make the turn back in time. The US safety board named fatigue and excessive workload among the probable causes, along with the company’s failure to provide a rested and sufficient crew. The lesson for me is not that one officer failed. It is that a system which relies on a tired person performing perfectly at the worst hour has already chosen to fail one night out of many. The decisions that sink a project are often made early and look like routine paperwork. So my rule is simple. Before a critical decision I check fitness the way I check the numbers. If the person deciding is not fit, including me, the decision waits or changes hands.
terms: Probable cause — the safety board’s formal finding of the main factors that led to an accident, as opposed to a finding of legal fault.
Excessive workload — more tasks than one person can perform reliably in the time available, a recognised contributor to error.
Single point of decision — one person whose error alone can cause a failure because no one else checks or relieves them.

hostile.q: Your whole project depends on you. What happens when you are exhausted at a critical moment?
hostile.a: I have named the critical watches on the project and a backup for each. Before I sign, pay or commit, I check how long I have been awake and whether this is the right hour. If I fail that check, the decision waits until I am fit or goes to the named backup. I would rather lose a day than make the project depend on my performing perfectly at four in the morning.

rule: Rule 4: Before a critical decision I check fitness the way I check the numbers, and if the person deciding is not fit, the decision waits or changes hands.

title: What a Tired Mistake Costs
summary: Fatigue does not show up as a line in a pro forma, but it moves cost, schedule and return through the errors it causes. This lesson prices a tired mistake two ways, as expected cost and as carrying cost, and shows how a lender reads the sponsor’s condition as part of the risk.
body:
A tired mistake is a cost like any other, it just arrives without an invoice. Price it as probability times impact, add the carrying cost of the delay it causes, and the case for protecting your best hours becomes arithmetic rather than wellness advice.

Recall

Q. What is reciprocity, and why does a negotiator use it?

A. Reciprocity is the strong pull to return a favour or concession. A negotiator makes a small early concession to create an obligation he can call on later, which is why you track concessions on both sides.

Q. What is the planning fallacy?

A. The tendency to underestimate cost and duration on your own plans even when you know similar projects ran over. The cure is the outside view: start from how the reference class actually performed.

Q. What was Rule 4?

A. Before a critical decision I check fitness the way I check the numbers, and if the person deciding is not fit, the decision waits or changes hands.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, a developer’s profit is the thin difference between what the project is worth and what it cost, including the cost of time. Small errors in contracts, draws, pricing or schedules move that difference directly. Most developers treat their own condition as a private matter. A lender does not. A lender is underwriting the sponsor as much as the building, because the building does not get finished by itself.

Expected cost: probability times impact

In plain English, the expected cost of a risk is how likely it is multiplied by how much it costs if it happens. You cannot know which particular decision will go wrong, but you can estimate how many will over a month, and what they cost on average.

The professional framing is expected value, the same tool an insurer or a reliability engineer uses. It turns a vague worry into a number you can compare with the cost of preventing it.

Worked example one. These are hypothetical, illustrative figures, not research results. Suppose you make 20 meaningful approvals a month: draws, change orders, contract clauses and price confirmations. Suppose that, made rested, 2 percent of them contain an error that costs money, and made tired, 6 percent do. Suppose the average error costs 50,000 dollars to put right.

  1. Rested: 20 approvals times 0.02 equals 0.4 errors a month. 0.4 times 50,000 dollars equals 20,000 dollars of expected cost.
  2. Tired: 20 times 0.06 equals 1.2 errors a month. 1.2 times 50,000 dollars equals 60,000 dollars.
  3. The difference is 40,000 dollars a month, or 480,000 dollars across a twelve-month build.

You do not need to believe those exact rates. Change them. Halve the gap and it is still 240,000 dollars a year. The point of the arithmetic is that a small change in error rate, multiplied across many decisions, buys a lot of protection: a later meeting, a paid backup reviewer, a rule that keeps signatures out of the night.

Say that out loud now.

Say it this way: a small error rate, times many decisions, times real money, is a large number.

Carrying cost: what the delay costs

The second way a mistake costs money is time. Fixing an error usually means waiting: for a revised drawing, a new price, a lender’s consent. While you wait, the loan accrues interest, the site costs money to keep, and your equity sits idle.

Worked example two, again hypothetical. You have drawn 5,000,000 dollars of a construction loan at an interest rate of 8 percent a year. A tired approval of an incomplete change order causes a 30-day delay while the scope is untangled.

  1. Interest for 30 days: 5,000,000 times 0.08 times 30 divided by 365 equals about 32,900 dollars.
  2. Add hypothetical site overheads of 25,000 dollars a month for security, temporary power, insurance and supervision. That is 25,000 dollars more.
  3. The direct carrying cost of the month is about 57,900 dollars, before any cost of the fix itself.

Now look at return. Suppose you invest 3,000,000 dollars of equity and expect to receive 5,000,000 dollars back after two years. Your equity multiple is 5,000,000 divided by 3,000,000, about 1.67 times. The annual return implied by one payment at the end, which is a simplified internal rate of return, is the square root of 1.67, minus 1, about 29 percent a year. The internal rate of return (IRR) is the annual rate at which the money you put in grows into the money you get back. Now suppose the error delays completion by three months and costs 100,000 dollars, so you receive 4,900,000 dollars after 2.25 years. The multiple falls to about 1.63, and the annual return falls to about 24 percent. A single mistake has taken roughly five percentage points off the return, mostly through time. Week 15 teaches these return measures properly; for now, notice that delay hurts return twice, once through cost and once through the calendar.

How the lender reads you

A lender cannot register a mortgage on your sleep, but the whole credit decision assumes the sponsor is functional. Lenders talk about key-person risk: the danger that a project depends on one individual whose absence, illness or poor judgment would put it in trouble. They look for a team, a backup, a monitor and a sponsor who answers questions crisply and on time. A sponsor who misses deadlines, contradicts himself on numbers or sends late-night messages full of errors is telling the lender something about key-person risk without meaning to. The commercial terms that follow, such as tighter covenants, more reporting and a larger equity requirement, are lender practice, not legal standards, and they vary by lender and market.

The biggest risk

The biggest financial risk is not one large mistake. It is a steady drift of small ones across a long build, each too small to notice, adding up to a missed margin. The control is to treat your decision quality as a managed input. Track approvals and errors in your decision journal, put the high-value approvals in your best hours, and pay for a second reviewer on anything above a threshold you set. As a hypothetical example, any change over 25,000 dollars gets a second set of eyes before you sign.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner thinks working through the night shows commitment and saves money. It usually spends money. A reviewer’s fee is small and known. An error in a draw or a contract is large and unknown. The beginner also hides fatigue from the lender, then contradicts his own numbers on a call. Saying "I will confirm that figure in writing by two o’clock" costs nothing and protects credibility; guessing costs both.

Callback

In Week 1 you saw that a developer pulls a small number of value levers: price, cost, time, risk and financing. Fatigue pulls three of them the wrong way at once. It adds cost through errors, adds time through rework, and adds risk through the lender’s view of you. That is why your physiology belongs in the same conversation as your budget.

Thread: time and energy on a rotating shift

A rotating schedule makes your energy a resource with a known shape, which is better than a resource with an unknown one. Map your rotation onto a calendar and mark three kinds of days: sharp days, usually your second and third days on a stable pattern; recovery days, after the switch back from nights; and red days, the mornings straight after night shifts. Put negotiation, drafting and review on sharp days. Put routine admin and reading on recovery days. Put nothing irreversible on red days.

Then protect the anchors. A regular wake-up window on days off, a consistent pre-sleep routine and a dark, cool room help most shift workers more than any single trick. If your rotation leaves you persistently sleepy, unable to sleep, or nodding off while driving, that pattern has a name in medicine, and it is worth raising. Check that with your doctor.

Recap

Price a tired mistake two ways. Expected cost is probability times impact, summed across many decisions. Carrying cost is the interest, overhead and lost return from the delay the mistake causes. Lenders read the sponsor’s reliability as key-person risk. Protect your decision quality like any other input: track it, schedule it and buy a second reviewer above a threshold.

Next: REGA, The Rules, on duty of care, hours of work and why a tired signature still binds you.
checklist: Count your meaningful approvals per month and estimate an honest error rate for rested and tired.
Price your average correctable error and compute the monthly expected-cost gap.
Compute the daily carrying cost of your current or planned loan balance.
Set a dollar threshold above which every change gets a second reviewer.
Mark sharp, recovery and red days on your rotation calendar.
Schedule negotiations and contract review only on sharp days.
Prepare a standard reply for lenders: confirm in writing by a stated time instead of guessing.
head: Field checklist
speak: A tired mistake is a cost that arrives without an invoice, and I price it two ways. First, expected cost: probability times impact. If I make twenty approvals a month and fatigue moves my error rate from two to six percent, on fifty-thousand-dollar errors that is forty thousand dollars a month of expected cost. Second, carrying cost: a mistake that delays a project a month on a five-million-dollar drawn balance at eight percent costs about thirty-three thousand dollars in interest alone, before overheads, and the delay cuts my annual return because time is in the denominator. A lender also reads my reliability as key-person risk, so errors and late-night contradictions cost me terms. My controls are practical: big approvals in my best hours, a second reviewer above a set threshold, and confirming figures in writing by a stated time instead of guessing.
terms: Expected cost — the probability of a loss multiplied by its size, used to compare a risk with the cost of preventing it.
Carrying cost — the interest, overhead and lost return incurred for each period a project is delayed.
Key-person risk — the danger that a project depends on one individual whose absence or poor judgment would put it in trouble.

hostile.q: You are one person with a day job on rotating shifts. Isn't this whole project key-person risk?
hostile.a: Yes, and I manage it as one. High-value approvals are scheduled for my sharp days, anything over a set threshold gets a second reviewer, the project has a named backup for each critical decision, and I report to you on a fixed calendar. I would rather show you the controls than ask you to rely on my stamina.

title: Tired Is Not a Defence: Duty, Hours and Your Signature
summary: The law rarely asks how tired you were; it asks what you owed, what you knew and what you signed. This lesson maps the general safety duty, hours-of-work rules and the signature rule as concepts, and shows how a developer turns them into contract terms and personal habits.
body:
Fatigue is almost never a legal defence, but it is often legal evidence. The law asks what duty you owed, what you knew about the hazard and what you put your name to, so the developer’s job is to build rest into his contracts and keep tired decisions out of his own signature.

Recall

Q. What is the difference between expected cost and carrying cost?

A. Expected cost is the probability of a loss times its size. Carrying cost is what each period of delay costs in interest, overhead and lost return.

Q. What is social proof, and when does it mislead a buyer?

A. Social proof is the pull to do what others appear to be doing. It misleads when the crowd is reacting to the same incomplete information you have, as in a frothy pre-sale market.

Q. What is an after-action review?

A. A short structured debrief after an event: what was supposed to happen, what actually happened, why there was a difference and what we will do next time.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, you will sit on both sides of fatigue law. As an owner and developer you engage contractors whose crews work long pours, night lifts and compressed schedules. As an individual you sign contracts, approve payments and drive home after shifts. In each role the question a regulator, court or counterparty asks is not how tired you felt. It is what you owed, what you knew and what you did about it. This lesson teaches concepts only. The rules differ by country, province and state, and they change. Verify every point against the primary source before you rely on it, and take local advice.

The general duty

Plain English: in most developed jurisdictions an employer must keep workers reasonably safe from hazards it knows about or should know about, even where no specific rule names the hazard.

The professional framing is the general duty. In the United States, federal occupational safety law contains a general duty requirement that sits beneath all the specific standards. Canadian provinces and territories have their own occupational health and safety statutes, which impose broad duties on employers, supervisors and, in many cases, on whoever controls a construction project. Fatigue is increasingly described by safety regulators as a recognised hazard, particularly for long hours, night work and safety-critical tasks. Verify the current wording and guidance in the jurisdiction where your site is.

Worked example one, hypothetical. Your contractor plans a continuous concrete pour on a transfer slab that will run 16 hours, staffed by one crew. Midway through, a tired operator misjudges a boom placement and a worker is injured. The regulator investigates. Questions will include: was fatigue a recognised hazard for this task, did the contractor have a plan for it, and what did the project owner know and require? If your contract and your meeting minutes show you required a fatigue plan, crew rotation and a supervisor check for any shift over 12 hours, you are in a far better position than if the record shows you pushed the schedule and said nothing. Whether an owner carries a legal duty here depends heavily on the jurisdiction and on how much control the owner exercises over the work. Professional sign-off required: lawyer practising occupational health and safety law in that jurisdiction.

Hours of work and rest

Plain English: many places set limits on working hours and minimum rest between shifts, and some industries have stricter rules of their own.

The professional framing has two layers. Employment standards legislation in many jurisdictions sets maximum hours, overtime rules and rest periods, often with exceptions and permits. Sector rules then sit on top for safety-critical work, such as hours-of-service limits for commercial drivers and duty limits for flight crews. You already know this pattern from grid operations, where operator duties are governed by their own standards and company rules. Construction generally relies on the general duty and employment standards rather than a single hours cap. Do not assume a number; look it up for the trade, the jurisdiction and the year.

Practical use: when you prequalify a contractor, ask how they manage hours on night work and long pours, and write the answer into the contract as a submittal requirement. You are not running their crew. You are making sure a plan exists and is recorded.

Say that out loud now.

Say it this way: the law asks what I owed, what I knew and what I signed, not how tired I felt.

The signature rule

Plain English: if you sign a contract, you are generally bound by it, whether or not you read it carefully and however tired you were.

The professional framing in common-law systems is often called the signature rule. A signature is treated as assent to the terms. The ways out are narrow: fraud, misrepresentation, mistake of a very specific kind, duress, or a lack of legal capacity, and each has demanding tests. Ordinary tiredness is not on that list. The same logic increasingly applies to email. Depending on the jurisdiction and the contract, a reply such as "approved, proceed" can be treated as a binding instruction or acceptance, and many construction contracts treat a written owner direction as a change the contractor is entitled to be paid for. Verify how your contract and your jurisdiction treat electronic approvals. Week 20 teaches contract formation properly.

Worked example two, hypothetical. At 05:10, after a night shift, you reply "Approved, go ahead" to a contractor’s email about extra rock excavation. The email had no price attached. Under a typical construction contract, you may have just directed changed work and left the price to be determined later, often at the contractor’s rates or by a valuation the contract sets. The contractor now has a written direction, which is exactly what a claim needs. The fix is cheap and habitual: during your red window, reply only "Received. I will respond by 14:00 with a decision and an agreed price." That sentence commits you to nothing except a time.

Driving, health and privacy

Two further points, briefly. First, falling asleep at the wheel can expose a driver to serious charges and to civil liability in many jurisdictions, and an employer who knowingly sends an exhausted worker on a long drive may face questions too. A short nap in a parked car before driving is a safety step, not a weakness. Second, a sleep disorder is a medical condition. Disclosure, privacy and any duty to accommodate are governed by health privacy and human rights or disability law, which vary by jurisdiction. Handle your own and your workers’ health information carefully, and take advice before acting on it.

The biggest risk

The biggest legal risk is an informal approval made in the red window that turns out to be binding, priced later at the other side’s rates. The control is a standard holding reply, a contract clause stating that only signed change orders in a set form bind the owner, and the discipline to use both. Even that clause is not a perfect shield, because conduct can sometimes waive it, so keep your conduct consistent with it.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner thinks safety is the contractor’s problem because the contractor employs the crew. In many jurisdictions owners who control a project, or who direct the schedule, attract duties of their own, and even where they do not, the record of what the owner demanded and ignored will be read closely after an incident. The beginner also thinks an email is not a contract. Sometimes it is exactly that.

Callback

In Week 1 you mapped every seat at the table and learned that the developer decides while others advise. This lesson adds the legal edge of that idea: the person who decides is the person whose signature, email and conduct get read afterwards. Your red window is not just a health habit. It is a records discipline.

Recap

Fatigue is rarely a defence and often evidence. Employers carry a general duty to manage recognised hazards, and fatigue is increasingly one of them. Hours rules exist in layers by jurisdiction and sector, so never assume a number. A signature, and often an email, binds you however tired you were. Build rest into contractor submittals, keep approvals in a set form, and use a holding reply in the red window. Verify every point against the primary source, and get local legal advice.

Next: Petra, The Numbers, working backward from a two o’clock meeting to plan sleep, light and caffeine after night shifts.
checklist: Identify the occupational safety statute and regulator for each jurisdiction where you build.
Add a fatigue management plan to the contractor safety submittal list.
Require crew rotation and a supervisor check for any operation planned over 12 hours.
Insert a clause that only signed change orders in a set form bind the owner.
Save your holding reply as a template for red-window messages.
Never approve work by email without a price, scope and reference number.
Take a short nap before driving if you are drowsy after a shift.
Book a meeting with a local lawyer to confirm owner duties before your first site starts.
head: Field checklist
speak: The law almost never asks how tired I was. It asks what I owed, what I knew and what I signed. Employers in most places carry a general duty to manage recognised hazards, and safety regulators increasingly treat fatigue as one of them, so as an owner I require a fatigue plan, crew rotation and supervisor checks for long pours and night work, and I keep the record. Hours-of-work rules exist in layers, by jurisdiction and by industry, so I never assume a number; I look it up. And a signature binds me however tired I was. Often an email does too, and a reply like approved, go ahead can direct changed work with the price left open. So in my red window I send one line: received, decision and agreed price by two o’clock. Every point here varies by jurisdiction, so I verify against the primary source and take local legal advice.
terms: General duty — a broad legal obligation on employers to protect workers from recognised hazards, even where no specific rule names the hazard.
Signature rule — the common-law principle that a person who signs a contract is generally bound by its terms whether or not they read them.
Owner direction — a written instruction from the owner that a contract may treat as a change the contractor is entitled to be paid for.

hostile.q: If one of my workers is hurt on a sixteen-hour pour, you will say safety was my problem. What did you as owner actually require?
hostile.a: Our contract required a fatigue management plan as a submittal, crew rotation and a supervisor check for any operation planned over twelve hours, and those requirements are in the minutes of the pre-pour meeting. I am not running your crew, but I made sure the plan existed, and I will not accept a schedule that depends on one crew working the whole pour.

title: Reverse Engineering a Sharp Two O’Clock
summary: A scheduler plans a project backward from the completion date; you can plan your body backward from the meeting that matters. This lesson works backward from a 14:00 lender meeting after a run of night shifts, then calculates how much of the afternoon’s caffeine is still in you at bedtime.
body:
Start from the finished outcome, a clear head at 14:00, and work backward through travel, caffeine, waking grogginess and sleep, exactly as a scheduler works back from a handover date. Then do the caffeine arithmetic forward to bedtime, because the dose that rescues the meeting can wreck the night after it.

Recall

Q. What is the signature rule?

A. The common-law principle that you are generally bound by what you sign, whether or not you read it and however tired you were. The exits, such as fraud or incapacity, are narrow.

Q. What does inversion ask?

A. Instead of asking how to succeed, it asks what would guarantee failure, and then you avoid those things. It surfaces risks that forward planning misses.

Q. What is the commitment and consistency principle?

A. People feel pressure to act consistently with what they have already said or done, so a small early commitment makes a larger later one more likely. Watch for it when a counterparty asks for small agreements first.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, you will not always choose when the important meeting falls. A lender, a council planner or a landowner will often set the time, and it will sometimes land the day after your last night shift. You can either arrive hoping for the best or arrive on a plan. Planning backward from the outcome is the scheduler’s core skill, and it works on the human body as well as it works on a building.

The method: work back from the milestone

In plain English, you fix the end point and ask, step by step, what must already be true just before it. A project scheduler calls this backward scheduling from a fixed milestone: you start at handover and work back through commissioning, finishes and structure to find the latest date each activity can start. Here the milestone is 14:00 on Thursday, and the activities are travel, caffeine, waking up properly and sleep.

Two physiological durations drive the plan, and both vary from person to person. First, sleep inertia: the grogginess after waking, which commonly lasts from several minutes to an hour or more and is worse when you wake from deep sleep. Second, caffeine’s rise: blood levels are commonly described as peaking within about an hour of drinking it. Treat both as approximate planning figures, not measurements of you.

Worked example one: the backward timeline

The scenario is hypothetical. You work night shifts from 19:00 to 07:00, and the last one ends at 07:00 on Thursday. The lender meeting is at 14:00 the same day, a 30-minute drive away.

StepLatest timeReasoning
Meeting starts14:00The fixed milestone.
Parked at the venue13:45Fifteen minutes for a few minutes of slow breathing in the parked car and a final look at your one page.
Leave home13:15Thirty-minute drive.
Caffeine13:00Rising toward its peak as the meeting starts.
Wake11:30Ninety minutes to clear sleep inertia: daylight, a shower, food, then one read-through of the numbers.
Asleep08:30A three-hour block, roughly two sleep cycles of about 90 minutes each, which makes waking from deep sleep less likely.
In bed08:15Dark, cool room, phone face down.
Home08:00Includes a short nap in the parked car before driving if you are drowsy at 07:15.
Shift ends07:00Handover complete.

Read the table from the bottom up and it is your Thursday. Read it from the top down and it is the logic. Notice the float, which is a scheduler’s word for slack. The only real float is in the drive home: if you nap 30 minutes instead of 15, you lose sleep, not the meeting. That tells you where the plan is fragile.

Say that out loud now.

Say it this way: I fix the milestone, then I work backward to the latest moment each step can start.

Two refinements. Common shift-work guidance suggests dark glasses on the morning drive home, because bright morning light tells the body clock the day has started and makes daytime sleep harder. And three hours is not a full night. The plan gets you sharp at 14:00; it does not repay your sleep debt. That is the job of Thursday night.

Worked example two: caffeine at bedtime

Now run the arithmetic forward. Caffeine leaves the body gradually. The half-life, meaning the time for the amount in your body to fall by half, is commonly cited as around five hours in healthy adults, but it varies widely with genetics, medications, smoking, pregnancy and liver function. Use five hours as a planning figure only, and check your own situation with your doctor.

You want to be asleep by 22:30 Thursday to return to a day pattern. You took a hypothetical 200 milligrams at 13:00, which is roughly a couple of cups of brewed coffee, though content varies a great deal by cup.

  1. Time elapsed from 13:00 to 22:30 is 9.5 hours.
  2. Number of half-lives elapsed is 9.5 divided by 5, which equals 1.9.
  3. Fraction remaining is one half raised to the power 1.9. One half to the power 1 is 0.5; to the power 2 is 0.25; to the power 1.9 is about 0.27.
  4. Caffeine remaining is 200 milligrams times 0.27, which is about 54 milligrams.

You would be going to bed with roughly a quarter of the afternoon dose still active, about the caffeine in a small cup of coffee. A controlled study in 2013 found that a large dose taken even six hours before bed still measurably disrupted sleep. So test the options. Halve the dose to 100 milligrams and bedtime holds about 27 milligrams. Keep 200 milligrams but take it at 12:00, and you have 10.5 hours, 2.1 half-lives, about 0.23 remaining, or roughly 47 milligrams. The cleanest option is the smaller dose, taken earlier, with daylight and movement doing part of the work.

When the backward plan says no

Backward scheduling also tells you when a milestone cannot be met. Run the same table for a meeting at 09:00 instead of 14:00. Parked by 08:45, leave home by 08:15, wake by 06:45 at the latest. But your shift ends at 07:00. The plan has negative float: the latest start for sleep is before the shift even finishes. A scheduler facing negative float does not hope; he changes the logic or moves the milestone. You do the same. Ask for the meeting to move to the afternoon or the next day, and ask the day before, with a reason about the work rather than about your fatigue. The arithmetic gives you the confidence to ask early instead of apologising late.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is the drive home after the last night shift, which is the most dangerous single step on this timeline for you and for others on the road. The control is a hard rule: if you notice heavy eyelids, drifting or missed exits, stop and nap before driving. Never use a breathing drill or any other technique to push through drowsiness at the wheel. If the drive is routinely dangerous, arrange another way home.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner plans forward: comes home, sleeps until the alarm, rushes, drinks a large coffee in the car and arrives groggy and over-caffeinated. Then he drinks more at 16:00 to stay up, cannot sleep Thursday night and starts Friday in debt. The backward plan fixes the morning; the forward caffeine arithmetic protects the night.

Callback

Three lessons ago you learned the two forces behind alertness: the body clock and sleep pressure. This plan works both. The three-hour sleep relieves some sleep pressure. Daylight after waking and darkness on the drive home nudge the body clock. Caffeine only masks pressure, which is why it gets a dose and a deadline rather than a free hand.

Recap

Fix the milestone and work backward: parked, travel, caffeine, wake, sleep, home, shift end. Find where the float is, because that is where the plan breaks. Then run caffeine forward to bedtime with the half-life arithmetic: elapsed hours divided by the half-life, one half to that power, times the dose. Every figure here is a planning estimate; check your own case with your doctor.

Next: Kema, The Room, holding your state through that 14:00 meeting.
checklist: Write the milestone first, then list each step backward with its latest start time.
Identify the float in the plan and decide what you will sacrifice if it is used.
Budget at least an hour after waking before any high-stakes conversation.
Wear dark glasses on the drive home after a night shift, if safe for you.
Nap in a parked car before driving whenever you notice drowsiness.
Calculate the caffeine remaining at your planned bedtime before taking the dose.
Prefer a smaller, earlier caffeine dose over a large late one.
Check your caffeine use, medications and sleep pattern with your doctor.
head: Field checklist
speak: When a meeting lands the day after night shifts, I plan backward from it the way a scheduler plans back from handover. Meeting at fourteen hundred. Parked by thirteen forty-five for a few minutes of slow breathing. Leave home at thirteen fifteen. Caffeine at thirteen hundred so it is rising as I walk in. Wake at eleven thirty, giving ninety minutes for grogginess to clear. Asleep by eight thirty for about two full sleep cycles. Home by eight, napping in the parked car first if I am drowsy. Then I run the caffeine forward. With a planning half-life of five hours, two hundred milligrams at one in the afternoon leaves about a quarter, roughly fifty milligrams, at ten thirty at night. So I take less, earlier. These are planning figures, not measurements of me, and I check my own case with my doctor.
terms: Backward scheduling — planning from a fixed end date by working out the latest moment each earlier step can start.
Sleep inertia — the grogginess and slowed thinking after waking, worse when woken from deep sleep.
Half-life — the time it takes for the amount of a substance in the body to fall by half.

hostile.q: We booked this meeting at two. You came off nights this morning. Should we really be doing this now?
hostile.a: Yes. I planned for it: I slept from half past eight, I have been up since half past eleven, and I have the numbers on one page. If anything you ask needs a figure I cannot stand behind right now, I will tell you so and confirm it in writing by a time we agree today.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: Holding Your State in the Two O’Clock Meeting
summary: A scene: a lender meeting the afternoon after night shifts. This lesson gives you the lines to say, the lines never to say, the question behind the question, when to stay silent, and three research-backed tools for holding your state: slow breathing while parked, reappraisal and a steady voice.
body:
In the room, the credit officer is not only judging your numbers; she is judging whether you are in control. You hold your state with three tools, slow breathing in the parked car, reappraising the nerves as fuel, and a slower, lower voice, and you protect your credibility by never guessing a number.

Recall

Q. In backward scheduling, how do you find where a plan is fragile?

A. You look for the float, the slack between steps. The place with little or no float is where a small slip breaks the milestone.

Q. What is a decision journal for?

A. To record, before a decision, what you expect, why and how confident you are, so you can later judge the quality of the decision separately from the luck of the outcome.

Q. Why does authority influence us, and how do you check it?

A. We tend to defer to titles and expertise. You check it by asking for the evidence behind the expert’s claim and whether the expert has a stake in the answer.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, most meetings that matter in development are short, and much of their outcome is decided by how the sponsor carries himself when he is under pressure. A lender, an investor or a council officer is quietly asking whether you will be steady when the project goes wrong. You will often walk in tired. You cannot fake rested, but you can be controlled, honest and precise, and that reads as strength.

The scene

This is a composite scene. It is Thursday at 14:00. You came off your last night shift at 07:00, slept three hours on the plan Petra built, and you are in a small meeting room at a bank with a credit officer and her analyst. She has your one-page summary in front of her. Ten minutes in, she says: "Walk me through your contingency. Twelve percent seems light for a building this size."

Your heart rate jumps. You feel the familiar pull to talk fast and fill the silence.

Holding your state: three tools

First, slow breathing, done in the parked car before you walk in, never while driving. Breathing out more slowly than you breathe in tends to calm the body’s alarm response. A simple pattern is in through the nose for about four seconds and out through the mouth for about six, which works out to six breaths a minute, for three to five minutes. Another is the physiological sigh: two short inhales through the nose, then one long, slow exhale. A small randomised study published in 2023 found that a few minutes a day of exhale-focused breathing improved mood more than a mindfulness exercise did. Treat that as promising, not proven, and check any breathing practice with your doctor if you have a heart or lung condition.

Second, reappraisal. Do not tell yourself to calm down; that rarely works under real pressure. Relabel the arousal. Laboratory studies by Jeremy Jamieson and colleagues found that people told that a racing heart helps performance did better on a demanding test, and Alison Wood Brooks found that saying "I am excited" before a stressful task beat trying to feel calm. The professional framing is stress reappraisal: the same body response, read as fuel instead of threat. In the room, the sentence in your head is: this is energy for the answer.

Third, voice. Fatigue and stress push the voice faster, higher and flatter, and sentences start to rise at the end as if they were questions. Slow down, let your sentences fall at the end, and pause after a number. A slow, falling sentence sounds like a decision.

Say that out loud now.

Say it slowly, letting the last word drop: this is energy for the answer.

The lines

Say this: "Fair question. The twelve percent is split into two parts: design contingency, which comes down as drawings complete, and construction contingency, held to the end. On the hard cost of eight million, that is 960,000 dollars. Our cost consultant reviewed it against similar projects, and I can send you that review." Then stop talking.

Notice the structure: acknowledge, answer, offer evidence, stop. It works because it does not argue with her, does not apologise and does not volunteer new problems.

If you do not know a figure: "I don’t want to give you a number from memory. I will confirm it in writing by 17:00 tomorrow." Then write it down in front of her and make sure it arrives on time.

Never say: "Sorry, I’m wrecked, I just came off nights." It invites her to discount everything else you say. Never say: "It’s probably around ten or twelve percent, I think." A guessed number from a sponsor is worse than no number. Never say: "Every lender asks that, it’s fine." Dismissing the concern tells her you will dismiss problems on site too. And never fill a silence with a fresh worry she did not ask about.

The question behind the question

Her literal question is about twelve percent. The question behind it is: does this sponsor understand where projects actually go over budget, and will he have the money when it happens? So your best answer touches that directly: who reviewed the contingency, against what evidence, and what happens if it runs out, such as a cost-overrun reserve or additional equity commitment. Commercial practice on contingency levels varies by lender, project type and stage of design; they are not standards, so do not quote a figure as the rule.

Worked example in the room. Suppose, hypothetically, hard cost is 8,000,000 dollars, design contingency is 5 percent and construction contingency is 7 percent. Design contingency is 0.05 times 8,000,000, which is 400,000 dollars. Construction contingency is 0.07 times 8,000,000, which is 560,000 dollars. Together, 960,000 dollars, which is 12 percent. If you can say those three numbers calmly, and in that order, you have shown structure as well as a total.

When to stay silent

Stay silent after you give a number. Stay silent while she reads. Stay silent after she states an objection, for a full breath, before you answer; it shows you heard it. The urge to fill silence is strongest when you are tired, which is exactly when filling it costs most.

And know when to move the meeting. A second worked example: suppose, before the meeting, you slept under four hours and the agenda is a negotiation where you must agree terms in the room. The rule is to move it at least a day ahead, by phone, with a reason that is about the work: "I want to come with the updated cost review; can we do Monday?" Move it the day before, not in the morning. A review meeting you can attend tired; a decision meeting you should not.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a confident guess that later proves wrong. One wrong number from a sponsor makes a lender re-check every other number. The control is the confirm-in-writing line, said without embarrassment, with a time attached and kept.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner tries to look calm by suppressing everything, goes stiff, talks fast anyway and ends sentences on a rising note. Composure is not the absence of nerves. It is nerves pointed at the job, with a slower voice and the discipline to stop talking.

Callback

In Week 3 you studied influence and trust. Trust in a lending room is built less by charm than by consistency: what you say matches the paper, what you promise arrives when you said it would, and what you do not know you say you do not know. The confirm-in-writing line is a trust-building tool disguised as an admission.

Recap

Before the room, breathe slowly in the parked car. In the room, relabel the nerves as energy, slow the voice and let sentences fall. Acknowledge, answer, offer evidence, stop. Hear the question behind the question. Never guess a number; confirm it in writing by a stated time. Move decision meetings, not review meetings, when you are under-slept.

Next: Kema, Quiz and Recap, with Cole in the Auditor’s Chair on a contractor’s fatigue plan.
checklist: Do three to five minutes of slow breathing in the parked car before a hard meeting.
Use one reappraisal sentence: this is energy for the answer.
Slow your pace and let sentences fall at the end.
Answer in four beats: acknowledge, answer, offer evidence, stop.
Never guess a number; say you will confirm it in writing by a stated time.
Stay silent for a full breath after an objection and after you give a figure.
Move decision meetings a day ahead if you slept under four hours; attend review meetings.
head: Field checklist
speak: In a lending room the officer is judging my numbers and also whether I am in control. I hold my state three ways. Before I go in, I breathe slowly in the parked car, longer out than in, for a few minutes. In the room, I relabel the nerves: this is energy for the answer. And I slow my voice and let my sentences fall at the end. When she challenges my contingency, I acknowledge, answer, offer evidence and stop: twelve percent, split between design and construction contingency, nine hundred and sixty thousand dollars on eight million of hard cost, reviewed by our cost consultant. The question behind her question is whether I will have the money when costs run over, so I answer that too. I never guess a number. If I do not have it, I confirm it in writing by a stated time and I keep that promise.
terms: Stress reappraisal — relabelling the body’s stress response as useful energy rather than a threat, which research links to better performance.
Physiological sigh — a breathing pattern of two short inhales followed by one long, slow exhale.
Question behind the question — the underlying concern that drives the literal question someone asks.

hostile.q: Your contingency is twelve percent. What happens when you burn through it in month eight?
hostile.a: Then the cost-overrun reserve and my additional equity commitment cover it, in that order, and you will see it coming in the monthly cost report well before month eight. The contingency is split into design and construction pots, it was reviewed against comparable projects by our cost consultant, and I will send you that review by five tomorrow.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: Week 4 Review: Fatigue, Caffeine, Breath and Voice
summary: Kema tests the week on physiology: the two forces behind alertness, the red window, caffeine arithmetic, Rule 4 and holding your state. Cole takes the Auditor’s Chair on a contractor’s fatigue management plan, and the boardroom drill asks you to explain the week in two minutes.
body:
This week’s single idea: your judgment runs on a body with a clock, a debt and an alarm, so you manage it with written rules, planned schedules and practised tools rather than with willpower. Today you test that idea, audit a document against it and say it aloud in two minutes.

Recall

Q. What three questions make up the fitness check before a critical decision?

A. How long have I been awake? Is this the right hour? Who else could take this?

Q. What is the rule of the outside view in one sentence?

A. Start from how similar projects actually turned out, then adjust for what is genuinely different about yours.

Q. In Week 1, what is a value lever?

A. One of the few things a developer can change to move a project’s value, such as price, cost, time, risk or financing.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, knowledge you cannot retrieve under pressure is decoration. This review is retrieval practice: answering from memory before checking, which research on learning consistently finds strengthens recall more than rereading. Answer each question aloud before you read the answer.

Use this lesson in three passes. First, cover the answers and say yours aloud. Second, mark any question you hesitated on and reread that day’s lesson, not the whole week. Third, in a week’s time, answer the six questions again without looking. Spacing the second attempt out is uncomfortable, and that discomfort is part of what makes the memory stick. Score yourself honestly: an answer you half-remembered counts as a miss, because in a meeting a half-remembered rule turns into a guess.

The six questions

Question 1: What two forces set your alertness at any hour?

Answer: The body clock, a roughly 24-hour rhythm with its low in the small hours, and sleep pressure, which builds with every hour awake.

Question 2: Why can you not trust your own sense of how tired you are?

Answer: Research shows that under repeated short sleep, performance keeps falling while felt sleepiness levels off, so feeling fine is what impairment feels like from inside.

Question 3: What is your red window?

Answer: A written rule naming the hours, such as overnight and straight after a night shift, in which you will not sign, pay or make new commitments.

Question 4: You take 200 milligrams of caffeine ten hours before bed. With a planning half-life of five hours, how much remains?

Answer: Ten hours is two half-lives, so one quarter remains: about 50 milligrams.

Question 5: What is Rule 4?

Answer: Before a critical decision I check fitness the way I check the numbers, and if the person deciding is not fit, the decision waits or changes hands.

Question 6: Why is an email reply sent at 05:00 a legal risk?

Answer: Depending on the contract and jurisdiction, a reply such as approved, go ahead can be a binding owner direction with the price left open, and tiredness is not a defence.

The week in one page

Day 1 set out the hardware. Two forces, the body clock and sleep pressure, set alertness. Short sleep damages performance while hiding its own effects, so you decide by rule, starting with a red window. Day 2, Ford took the Exxon Valdez through seven steps: a reasonable ice diversion became an unavoidable grounding in minutes, but the causes, including fatigue and crewing, were laid down long before. Day 3, Roman priced a tired mistake as expected cost and carrying cost, and showed how a lender reads sponsor reliability as key-person risk. Day 4, REGA set out the rules: the general duty to manage recognised hazards, layered hours-of-work rules, and the signature rule that binds you however tired you were. Day 5, Petra planned a sharp 14:00 backward from the milestone and ran caffeine forward to bedtime. Day 6 put you in the room with breathing, reappraisal and voice.

The Auditor’s Chair

This week Cole takes the Red Pen and reads as a hostile auditor would: assume the document will be relied on after an incident, and look for anything that would not survive cross-examination. Here is a hypothetical excerpt from a contractor’s fatigue management plan, submitted for a residential tower.

Section 4, Fatigue. Workers may work extended hours as needed to maintain the schedule. Supervisors will monitor workers for signs of fatigue. Workers who feel tired are encouraged to take a break. Night pours will be staffed by the day crew where practical. This plan has been reviewed and approved by management.

Read it twice and mark every defect before reading on.

Say that out loud now.

Say each defect aloud as you find it, then compare.

Cole’s findings. First, "extended hours as needed" sets no limit, so the schedule, not safety, decides. An auditor wants a number for maximum shift length and minimum rest between shifts, consistent with local law. Second, "supervisors will monitor" names no method and creates no record; after an incident, there is no evidence it ever happened. An auditor wants a named check, such as a pre-task fitness question, and a log. Third, "workers who feel tired" relies on self-report, which this week showed is unreliable, and offers no protection against being penalised for speaking up. Fourth, "night pours will be staffed by the day crew where practical" is the most dangerous sentence on the page: it plans for exactly the long, overnight, fatigued operation the Exxon Valdez warns about, and "where practical" is an escape hatch. An auditor wants a separate or relieved crew and a stated plan for long operations. Fifth, "reviewed and approved by management" names no person, no date and no version. The control for all five: return the plan with numbered comments and require limits, named checks, logs, crew rotation for long operations and a signed, dated revision before the work starts.

The boardroom drill

Set a timer for two minutes and explain this week to an imagined board of your own company. Then compare with the model.

Model answer: "Our biggest operational risk is not the building; it is decision quality at the wrong hour. Alertness is set by the body clock and by hours awake, and people underestimate their own impairment. So we run three controls. First, a red window: no signatures, payments or new commitments overnight or straight after a night shift; urgent items get a holding reply and an answer by a stated time. Second, critical decisions get a fitness check and a named backup. Third, our contractors submit fatigue plans with hour limits, logged checks and crew rotation for long pours. The cost case is simple: small error rates across many approvals, plus the carrying cost of delay, add up to more than the controls cost. And in the room, I never guess a number; I confirm it in writing by a stated time."

The biggest risk

The biggest risk after a week like this is treating it as wellness advice and letting it fade. The control is to turn it into paper this week: write the red window, add the sleep line to your decision journal and add the fatigue plan to your contractor submittal list.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner hears "physiology" and assumes it is soft. It is the opposite. Fatigue appears in accident findings, in legal records and in a lender’s view of key-person risk. Treat it with the same seriousness as a structural load.

Callback

In Week 2 you learned the after-action review: what was supposed to happen, what happened, why the difference, what next. Use it on your next run of night shifts. The difference between your plan and your actual Thursday is data, and it will tell you where your own float really is.

Recap

Your body has a clock, a debt and an alarm. Manage them with a red window, a fitness check, a backward plan and three tools for the room: slow breathing while parked, reappraisal and a slower voice. Audit others’ fatigue plans for limits, checks, records and rotation.

checklist: Question 1: What two forces set your alertness at any hour? Answer: The body clock, a roughly 24-hour rhythm with its low in the small hours, and sleep pressure, which builds with every hour awake.

Question 2: Why can you not trust your own sense of how tired you are? Answer: Research shows that under repeated short sleep, performance keeps falling while felt sleepiness levels off, so feeling fine is what impairment feels like from inside.
Question 3: What is your red window? Answer: A written rule naming the hours, such as overnight and straight after a night shift, in which you will not sign, pay or make new commitments.

Question 4: You take 200 milligrams of caffeine ten hours before bed. With a planning half-life of five hours, how much remains? Answer: Ten hours is two half-lives, so one quarter remains: about 50 milligrams.
Question 5: What is Rule 4? Answer: Before a critical decision I check fitness the way I check the numbers, and if the person deciding is not fit, the decision waits or changes hands.

Question 6: Why is an email reply sent at 05:00 a legal risk? Answer: Depending on the contract and jurisdiction, a reply such as approved, go ahead can be a binding owner direction with the price left open, and tiredness is not a defence.
head: The six questions
speak: This week was about the hardware behind my judgment. Two forces, the body clock and sleep pressure, set how alert I am, and short sleep damages performance while hiding itself, so I decide by rule rather than by feel. My red window keeps signatures, payments and new commitments out of the night and the hours after a night shift. Before any critical call I check how long I have been awake, whether this is the right hour and who else could take it. The money case is simple: small error rates across many approvals, plus the carrying cost of delay, add up fast. Legally, a tired signature or a quick email still binds me. I plan sharp meetings backward from the milestone, and I run caffeine forward to bedtime. In the room I breathe slowly while parked, treat nerves as energy, slow my voice and never guess a number.
terms: Retrieval practice — recalling information from memory before checking it, which strengthens learning more than rereading.
Auditor’s Chair — reading a document as a hostile auditor would, assuming it will be relied on after something goes wrong.
Escape hatch — a phrase such as where practical that lets a party avoid an obligation the document appears to create.

hostile.q: Your contractor’s fatigue plan says supervisors will monitor workers. Isn’t that enough?
hostile.a: No. It names no method, sets no limit and creates no record, so after an incident there is no evidence it happened. I return plans like that with comments and require maximum shift lengths, minimum rest, a named pre-task check with a log, crew rotation for long pours and a signed, dated revision before the work starts.
